extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical philosophy / readers of Plato
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of Plato's Republic Book IX
extracted.subtask_description: Close interpretive commentary and thematic analysis of material in Plato's Republic (esp. the Platonic number puzzles and Book IX on the tyrant, pleasure, and the soul). Emphasises textual, mathematical, and historical evidence used to read difficult passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of the two nations in one
rubrics_metrics.description: “the description of the two nations in one, which become more and more divided in the Greek Republics, as in feudal times, and perhaps also in our own;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author highlights this as a major theme to note in Plato: the split or duality within a polity that tends to widen. Treat as a structural motif when reading the Republic (compare historical analogies such as Greek Republics and feudal societies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notion of democracy as 'equality among unequals'
rubrics_metrics.description: “the notion of democracy expressed in a sort of Pythagorean formula as equality among unequals;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take Plato's formulation as a diagnostic for his critique of democracy: the idea that democracy levels inherently unequal individuals. Use this phrase to evaluate democratic passages and Plato's normative stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty characterised by free and easy ways of men and animals
rubrics_metrics.description: “the free and easy ways of men and animals, which are characteristic of liberty, as foreign mercenaries and universal mistrust are of the tyrant;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast imagery of liberty (ease, animal comparatives) with imagery of tyranny (mercenaries, mistrust) when assessing Plato's moral and political portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal that mere debts should not be recoverable by law
rubrics_metrics.description: “the proposal that mere debts should not be recoverable by law is a speculation which has often been entertained by reformers of the law in modern times, and is in harmony with the tendencies of modern legislation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this legal-proposal-as-speculation as an example of Plato's practical reforms; compare to modern reform debates about enforceability of debts and legislative tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayals of individual character-types (timocratical, oligarchical, democratic, tyrannical)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the family picture of the father and mother and the old servant of the timocratical man, and the outward respectability and inherent meanness of the oligarchical; the uncontrolled licence and freedom of the democrat ... and there is the wild-beast nature, which breaks loose in his successor. ... The hit about the tyrant being a parricide; the representation of the tyrant’s life as an obscene dream; the continuous image of the drones ... are among Plato’s happiest touches.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read Plato's individual portraits as deliberate, diagnostic character sketches that embody political types. Use these scenes/striking images as evidence for claims about each regime/type rather than as incidental detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Platonic 'number of the State' is a major interpretive difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: “There remains to be considered the great difficulty of this book of the Republic, the so-called number of the State. This is a puzzle ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach numeric passages (the Platonic number) as significant and puzzling: do not dismiss as mere obscurity. Expect reference to mathematical/ Pythagorean ideas; treat as intentionally symbolic or technical rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for understanding the Platonic number: textual and mathematical cross-checks
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our hope of understanding the passage depends principally on an accurate study of the words themselves; on which a faint light is thrown by the parallel passage in the ninth book. Another help is the allusion in Aristotle, who makes the important remark that the latter part of the passage ... describes a solid figure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting obscure numerical passages: (a) study precise wording; (b) consult parallel passages within Plato; (c) consult Aristotle and ancient commentators; (d) bring in knowledge of Greek mathematics/Pythagorean symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a perfect (cyclical) number
rubrics_metrics.description: “Plato begins by speaking of a perfect or cyclical number (Tim.), i.e. a number in which the sum of the divisors equals the whole; this is the divine or perfect number in which all lesser cycles or revolutions are complete.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mathematical definition (sum of proper divisors equals the number) when Plato or commentators invoke 'perfect' or 'cyclical' number; treat it as the conceptual basis for 'divine' cycles in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the human or imperfect number and its structure
rubrics_metrics.description: “He also speaks of a human or imperfect number, having four terms and three intervals of numbers which are related to one another in certain proportions; these he converts into figures, and finds in them when they have been raised to the third power certain elements of number, which give two ‘harmonies,’ the one square, the other oblong;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret Platonic 'imperfect' number as a structured sequence (four terms, three intervals) convertible to geometric figures and harmonies (square/oblong); expect references to musical intervals and geometric/combinatorial constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Pythagorean triangle (3,4,5) and musical harmonies in numerical symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some further clue may be gathered from the appearance of the Pythagorean triangle, which is denoted by the numbers 3, 4, 5 ... The harmony of the musical scale, which is elsewhere used as a symbol of the harmony of the state, is also indicated. For the numbers 3, 4, 5 ... denote the intervals of the scale.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When numbers like 3,4,5 occur, read them both geometrically (right triangle) and musically (interval ratios). Plato often uses numerical/musical analogies to signal political/ethical harmonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive hypothesis: 216 as the Platonic number of births (imperfect cycle)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The second is the number of generations or births, and presides over them ... This is probably the number 216.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider 216 (=6^3) as a plausible candidate for Plato's 'human' number; evaluate this hypothesis against mathematical coincidences, Pythagorean traditions, and ancient references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual plausibility arguments linking numerical values to historical/population data (e.g., 8000, 400, 7600, 5040)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The explanation given ... supposes the two harmonies to make up the number 8000. This explanation derives a certain plausibility from the circumstance that 8000 is the ancient number of the Spartan citizens ... The first harmony of 400, ... might be a symbol of the guardians—the larger or oblong harmony, of the people ... The number 5040, which is the number of the citizens in the Laws, is expressly based ... the convenience of the number for division; it is also made up of the first seven digits multiplied by one another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known ancient figures (e.g., Spartan citizen counts, 5040 in Laws) as circumstantial evidence when assessing Plato's numeric symbolism. Check for utilitarian/arithmetical reasons (divisibility) as well as symbolic ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary and technical sense for terms (terms/intervals/base, commensurable/irrational, waxing/waning)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The words ‘terms’ or ‘notes,’ and ‘intervals,’ are applicable to music as well as to number and figure. ... 'base' or 'fundamental number' ... 'squared and cubed' ... 'like and unlike' ... 'waxing' numbers ... 'waning' numbers ... 'commensurable' ... 'irrational' ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading the passage, understand technical Greek mathematical/musical vocabulary; many words have double application (music/arithmetical geometry). Accurate sense of these terms is crucial to interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit reasons offered for accepting the 216-interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Author lists reasons: (1) coincidence with description in first part; (2) familiar to a Greek mathematician; (3) 216 = 6^3 and sum of 3^3+4^3+5^3; (4) period of Pythagorean Metempsychosis; (5) matches musical scale positions; (6) product of cubes of 2 and 3; (7) attestation by Plutarch/Proclus/Quintilian; (8) triangle called figure of marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these enumerated points as the evidentiary standard used by the commentator to argue for 216. When assessing the claim, weigh mathematical coincidences, cultural/Pythagorean doctrines, and ancient testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plato’s account of pleasure: moderation and superiority of intellectual pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: “Plato’s account of pleasure is remarkable for moderation ... he is not, like the Cynics, opposed to all pleasure ... he now observes that there are a further class of ‘wild beast’ pleasures ... He dwells upon the relative and unreal character of sensual pleasures ... pointing out the superiority of the pleasures of reason, which are at rest, over the fleeting pleasures of sense and emotion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read Plato as distinguishing genuine (intellectual) pleasures from spurious sensual ones; interpret his ethics in light of the soul’s parts and the stability/knowledge-bearing character of intellectual pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of pleasure corresponding to parts of the soul and their hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: “The second [proof] is derived from the three kinds of pleasure, which answer to the three elements of the soul—reason, passion, desire; ... And so we arrive at the result that the pleasure of the rational part of the soul, and a life passed in such pleasure is the pleasantest. ... Next comes the life of ambition, and, in the third place, that of money-making.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the triadic schema (reason > passion/ambition > desire/avarice) as a criterion for evaluating lives and regimes. The commentator treats experiential knowledge and scope of judgement as decisive for ranking pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is not merely absence of pain; pure pleasures exist
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is not, like the Cynics, opposed to all pleasure, but rather desires that the several parts of the soul shall have their natural satisfaction; he even agrees with the Epicureans in describing pleasure as something more than the absence of pain. ... there are pleasures which have no antecedent pains ... Pure pleasure then is not the absence of pain, nor pure pain the absence of pleasure;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting Plato’s account of pleasure, do not reduce pleasure to mere absence of pain. Recognise pleasures that are positive (smell, hope, intellectual delight) and treat contrast/anticipation effects carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical measure of the interval between king and tyrant: 729
rubrics_metrics.description: “The number of the interval which separates the king from the tyrant, and royal from tyrannical pleasures, is 729, the cube of 9. ... The oligarch, again, is thrice removed from the king, and thus we get the formula 3 x 3, which is the number of a surface, representing the shadow which is the tyrant’s pleasure, and if you like to cube this ‘number of the beast,’ you will find that the measure of the difference amounts to 729; the king is 729 times more happy than the tyrant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take Plato's numerical illustration seriously as an expressive (arithmetical) device: 729 is offered as a figurative measure of comparative happiness. Use the cube/square metaphors to trace Plato's ordinal removals between regime-types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image of the soul as composite beasts (many-headed beast / lion / man) to illustrate justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “Fashion a multitudinous beast, having a ring of heads ... Suppose now another form of a lion, and another of a man; ... join them together and cover them with a human skin ... the maintainer of justice ... is trying to strengthen the man; he is nourishing the gentle principle within him, and making an alliance with the lion heart, in order that he may be able to keep down the many-headed hydra ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite image as an interpretive tool: justice aims to foster the human/divine principle and align it with spirited elements to control base appetites. Read ethical prescriptions as psychologically structured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational and legal aim: cultivate self-control and the higher principle
rubrics_metrics.description: “The real disgrace of handicraft arts is, that those who are engaged in them have to flatter, instead of mastering their desires; therefore we say that they should be placed under the control of the better principle in another ... And our intention in educating the young, is to give them self-control; the law desires to nurse up in them a higher principle, and when they have acquired this, they may go their ways.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider Plato’s pedagogy and law as instruments to cultivate self-mastery: education and legislation are judged by their capacity to nurture the higher principle and restraint of appetites.
